The royal city of that Blessed One was named Haṃsavatī. His father was the khattiya King Ānanda, and his mother was named Sujātā. Devala and Sujāta were the two chief disciples. The monk named Sumana was his attendant. Amitā and Asamā were the two chief female disciples. The Salala (Sal) tree was his Bodhi tree. He was eighty-eight cubits in height. His bodily radiance spread and remained for twelve yojanas all around. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

After the time of that Blessed One, after seventy thousand kappas had passed, thirty thousand kappas ago from this present age, two Buddhas named Sumedha and Sujāta appeared in a single kappa. For the Blessed One Sumedha also, there were three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly at the city of Sudassana, there were one hundred crores of Arahants; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Brahmin youth named Uttara. He gave away eighty crores of wealth that had been buried and stored, and after giving a great gift to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, he listened to the Dhamma, established himself in the refuges, went forth from the world, and became a monk. That Blessed One Sumedha also prophesied to that youth Uttara, "In the future, you will become a Buddha."

The royal city of the Blessed One Sumedha was named Sudassana. His father was the king named Sudatta, and his mother was also named Sudattā. Saraṇa and Sabbakāma were the two chief disciples. The monk named Sāgara was his attendant. Rāmā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples. The Mahānīpa tree was his Bodhi tree. He was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

After the time of that Blessed One, the Teacher named Sujāta appeared. For that Blessed One also, there were three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly, six million monks...
66:
(Assemblies of disciples) occurred; in the second assembly, there were five million (monks), and in the third assembly, four million (monks). At that time, the Bodhisatta became a Cakkavatti (Universal Monarch). Having heard that "A Buddha has arisen," he approached and listened to the Dhamma. He then offered the sovereignty of the four great islands along with the seven treasures to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha and ordained in the presence of the Teacher. All the citizens of the country, taking up the state duties and fulfilling the tasks of monastery attendants, constantly offered great alms to the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. That Teacher also gave a prophecy to that Cakkavatti.

The city of that Blessed One was named Sumangala. His father was King Uggata, and his mother was named Pabhāvatī. Sudassana and Sudeva were the two chief disciples. Nārada was the attendant. Nāgā and Nāgasamālā were the two chief female disciples. The Mahāveḷu (Great Bamboo) was the Bodhi tree. It is said that the Bodhi tree had a small hollow and a solid trunk, and it was beautiful like a bundle of peacock feathers with its large branches spreading upwards. The body of that Blessed One was fifty cubits high, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

In the period after that Blessed One, counting from this aeon, in one aeon one hundred and eighteen aeons ago, three Buddhas named Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī were born. For the Buddha Piyadassī also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a youth named Kassapa, who had mastered the three Vedas. Having listened to the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, he renounced one hundred thousand crores of wealth, built and offered a Saṅghārāma monastery, and established himself in the refuges and the precepts. Then the Teacher gave him a prophecy, saying, "After one hundred and eighteen aeons, you will become a Buddha."

The city of that Blessed One was named Anoma. His father was King Sudinna, and his mother was named Candā. Pālita and Sabbadassī were the two chief disciples. Sobhita was the attendant. Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were the two chief female disciples. The Piyaṅgu tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was eighty cubits high, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

In the period after that Blessed One, the Blessed One named Atthadassī arose. For him also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were nine million eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, eight million eight hundred thousand; and likewise in the third, there were (eight million eight hundred thousand). At that time, the Bodhisatta...
67:
...became a powerful ascetic named Susīma. Having brought a Mandārava celestial flower parasol from the deva world, he worshipped the Teacher. That Teacher also gave a prophecy to that ascetic (that he would become a Buddha in the future).

The city of that Blessed One was named Sobhaṇa. His father was the king named Sāgara, and his mother was named Sudassanā. The two chief disciples were Santa and Upasanta. The attendant was named Abhaya. The two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā. The Bodhi tree was the Campaka tree. The height of his body was eighty cubits. The radiance of his body spread and remained for about one yojana all around at all times. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

In the period after that, the Teacher named Dhammadassī arose. For him also, there were three assemblies of disciples (Saṅghasannipāta). In the first assembly, there were one hundred crores of monks; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, King of Devas, and he made offerings with divine perfumes and flowers, as well as with divine musical instruments. That Teacher also gave a prophecy to that Sakka.

The city of that Blessed One was named Saraṇa. His father was the king named Saraṇa, and his mother was named Sunandā. The two chief disciples were Paduma and Phussadeva. The attendant was named Sunetta. The two chief female disciples were Khemā and Sabbanāmā. The Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree; it was also called the 'Kakudha tree' or the 'Bimbijāla tree'. The height of his body was eighty cubits. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

In the period after that, ninety-four aeons from now, in one aeon, a single Buddha named Siddhattha arose. For him also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand crores of monks; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic named Mangala, endowed with sharp power and the strength of supernormal knowledges (abhiññā). Having brought a large Jambu (rose-apple) fruit, he offered it to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, after consuming that fruit, gave a prophecy to the Bodhisatta, saying, "Ninety-four aeons from now, you will become a Buddha."
68:
The city of that Blessed One was named Vebhāra. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Suphassā. Sambhala and Sumitta were the two chief disciples. The monk named Revata was the attendant. Sīvalā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples. The Kaṇikāra tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was sixty cubits in height. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

In the period following that Buddha, ninety-two aeons from now, two Buddhas named Tissa and Phussa appeared in a single aeon. For the Blessed One Tissa, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred crores of monks; in the second, ninety crores; and in the third, eighty crores. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a kshatriya named Sujāta, who possessed great wealth and fame. Having gone forth as a hermit and attained great psychic power, upon hearing that 'a Buddha has arisen,' he took celestial Mandārava, Paduma, and Pāricchattaka flowers and worshipped the Tathāgata as He walked in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Those flowers remained in the sky as a floral canopy. That Blessed One also prophesied of him: 'Ninety-two aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

The city of that Blessed One was named Khema. His father was the kshatriya Janasandha, and his mother was Padumā. Brahmadeva and Udaya were the two chief disciples. The monk named Samaṅga was the attendant. Phussā and Sudattā were the two chief female disciples. The Asana tree (Pitaunk) was the Bodhi tree. His body was sixty cubits in height. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

In the period following that Buddha, the Teacher named Phussa appeared. For him also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were six million monks; in the second, five million; and in the third, three million two hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a kshatriya named Vijitāvī. Having renounced a great kingdom and gone forth in the presence of the Teacher, he learned the three Pitakas and preached the Dhamma to the multitude. He also fulfilled the perfection of virtue (sīla-pāramī). That Blessed One also prophesied of him: 'You will become a Buddha.'

The city of that Blessed One was named Kāsi. His father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Sirimā. Surakkhita and Dhammasena were the two chief disciples. The monk named Sabhiya was the attendant. Cālā and Upacālā were the two chief female disciples...
69:
...were the chief female disciples. The Āmalaka tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height. His lifespan was ninety thousand years.

In the period following that Blessed One Phussa, ninety-one aeons from now, the Blessed One named Vipassī appeared. For that Blessed One also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were six million eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, one hundred thousand; and in the third, eighty thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a Naga king named Atula, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. He offered to the Blessed One a great golden throne adorned with the seven kinds of gems. That Blessed One also prophesied of that Bodhisatta: 'Ninety-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

The city of that Blessed One was named Bandhumatī. King Bandhumā was his father. Queen Bandhumatī was his mother. Khaṇḍa and Tissa were the two chief disciples. The monk named Asoka was the attendant. Candā and Candamittā were the two chief female disciples. The Pāṭali tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was eighty cubits in height. The radiance of his body always spread and remained for seven yojanas. His lifespan was eighty thousand years.

In the period following that Blessed One, thirty-one aeons from now, two Buddhas named Sikhī and Vessabhū appeared. For the Blessed One Sikhī also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand monks; in the second, eighty thousand; and in the third, seventy thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama. Having offered a great gift of robes and other requisites to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and having offered an elephant-treasure adorned with the seven kinds of gems, he then gave allowable items (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) equivalent in value to the elephant. That Blessed One also prophesied of that Bodhisatta: 'Thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha.'

The city of that Blessed One was named Aruṇavatī. The kshatriya Aruṇavā was his father. Queen Pabhāvatī was his mother. Abhibhū and Sambhava were the two chief disciples. The monk named Khemaṅkara was the attendant. Sakhilā and Padumā were the two chief female disciples. The Puṇḍarīka tree was the Bodhi tree. His body was seventy cubits in height. The radiance of his body spread and remained for three yojanas. His lifespan was seventy thousand years.

In the period following that Blessed One, the Teacher named Vessabhū appeared. For him also, there were three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were eighty thousand monks...
70:
In the second assembly of disciples, there were seventy thousand monks; in the third, sixty thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Sudassana. Having offered a great gift, including robes, to the Saᅅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he went forth as a monk in the presence of the Teacher. Being endowed with the virtue of conduct, he was full of reverence and joy in the Jewel of the Buddha. That Blessed One also gave him the prophecy: "Thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha."

The royal city of that Blessed One was named Anoma; his father was King Suppatģta, and his mother was named Yasavatģ. Soᅇa and Uttara were the two chief disciples; Upasanta was the attendant; Dāmā and Samālā were the two chief female disciples. The Sāla tree was his Bodhi tree. His height was sixty cubits, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.

After that time, in this aeon (kappa), four Buddhas have appeared: Kakusandha, Koᅇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One (Gotama). For the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was one assembly of disciples, in which there were forty thousand monks. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Khema. Having offered a great gift, including bowls and robes, as well as medicines such as collyrium to the Saᅅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, he heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching and went forth as a monk. That Teacher also gave him the prophecy.

The royal city of the Blessed One Kakusandha was named Khema; his father was a Brahmin named Aggidatta, and his mother was a Brahmin woman named Visākhā. Vidhura and Sajģva were the two chief disciples; Buddhija was the attendant; Sāmā and Campā were the two chief female disciples. The great Mahāsirģsa tree was his Bodhi tree. His height was forty cubits, and his lifespan was forty thousand years.

After that time, the Teacher named Koᅇāgamana appeared. For him also, there was one assembly of disciples, in which there were thirty thousand monks. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Pabbata. Surrounded by a host of ministers, he went to the presence of the Teacher, heard the Dhamma teaching, and invited the Saᅅgha of monks headed by the Buddha. Having offered a great gift, he also donated cloths from Pattuᅇᅇa, cloths from Cģna, silk cloths, woolen blankets, and fine linen cloths, as well as golden sandals, and went forth as a monk in the presence of the Teacher. That Teacher also gave him the prophecy.

The royal city of that Blessed One was named Sobhavatģ; his father was a Brahmin named Yāadatta, and his mother was a Brahmin woman named Uttarā. Bhiyyosa and...
71:
Uttara were the two chief disciples. There was an attendant named Sotthija. Samuddā and Uttarā were the two chief female disciples. The Udumbara tree was his Bodhi tree. His height was thirty cubits, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.

After that Blessed One Koᅇāgamana, the Teacher named Kassapa appeared. For that Blessed One also, there was only one assembly of disciples, in which there were twenty thousand monks. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a young Brahmin named Jotipāla, who had reached the further shore of the three Vedas and was well-known both on earth and in the sky. He was a friend of Ghaᅡģkāra the potter. Together with him, he approached the Teacher, heard the Dhamma talk, and went forth as a monk. Being possessed of exerted effort, he learned the three Pitakas and adorned the Buddha’s Dispensation by the fulfillment of major and minor duties. That Blessed One Kassapa also gave the prophecy to the young man Jotipāla: "In the future, you will become a Buddha."

The city of birth of that Blessed One was named Bārāᅇasģ. The Brahmin named Brahmadatta was his father; the Brahmin woman named Dhanavatģ was his mother. Tissa and Bhāradvāja were the two chief disciples. There was an attendant named Sabbamitta. Anuᄷā and Uruveᄷā were the two chief female disciples. The Nigrodha (Banyan) tree was his Bodhi tree. His height was twenty cubits, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years.

After that Blessed One Kassapa, excluding our present Sammāsambuddha, there is no other Buddha. Thus, the Bodhisatta, having received the prophecy in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dģpaᅅkara, said:

"Human birth, the male sex, the possession of sufficient cause, the sight of a Teacher,
Going forth, the possession of virtues, extreme dedication, and strong will—
Only when these eight conditions are combined does the aspiration (for Buddhahood) succeed."

Having combined these eight conditions, the Bodhisatta, who had made his aspiration at the feet of the Buddha Dģpaᅅkara, exerted effort, saying, "Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make one a Buddha." While searching, he saw the first perfection, the Perfection of Generosity (Dāna-pāramģ). He continued to fulfill those qualities that make one a Buddha, such as the Perfection of Generosity, until he reached the existence of King Vessantara. While proceeding through these lives, the following benefits were praised for those Bodhisattas who have made their aspiration:
72:
Thus, those who are complete in all factors and are certain of enlightenment (Bodhi), even though they wander in saṃsāra for a long period of hundreds of millions of aeons (kappas)—

They are not reborn in the Avīci hell, nor are they reborn in the Lokantara hells. They do not become Nijjhāmataṇhika petas, Khuppipāsika petas, or Kālakañjika asuras.

Even if they reach a woeful state (duggati), they do not become small, inferior animals. When born in the human realm, they are not born blind from birth.

They do not have deafness, nor do they become mute or crippled. They do not become female, nor do they become hermaphrodites (ubhatobyañjanaka) or eunuchs (paṇḍaka).

Those who are certain of enlightenment do not belong to [the lower classes of beings]. They are free from the five heinous crimes with immediate results (ānantarika-kamma), and in all births, they possess pure conduct (ācāra).

Because they see kamma and its results, they do not follow wrong views (micchā-diṭṭhi). Even though they may dwell in the celestial realms, they are not reborn in the realm of unconscious beings (asaññasatta).

There is no cause (the fruit of Anāgāmī) for them to be born in the Suddhāvāsa Brahma realms. These Great Beings (Bodhisattas), who are virtuous and whose minds are inclined towards renunciation (nekkhamma), do not cling to various existences; they practice for the benefit of the world and fulfill all the Perfections (pāramīs).

That Bodhisatta came only after attaining those advantages. For that Bodhisatta who was fulfilling the Perfections, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), such as in the times of Akitti the Brahmin, Saṅkha the Brahmin, King Dhanañjaya, King Mahāsudassana, Mahāgovinda, King Nimi, Prince Candakumāra, Visayha the Merchant, King Sivi, and King Vessantara. However, specifically in the Sasa-Paṇḍita Jātaka—

"Seeing one who approached for alms-food, I sacrificed my own self. There is no one equal to me in giving; this is my Perfection of Giving."

Because of such sacrifice of his own self, the Perfection of Giving became the Ultimate Perfection of Giving (dāna-paramattha-pāramī).
73:
Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Virtue (sīla-pāramī), such as in the times of being Sīlavanāga the Elephant King, Campeyya the Naga King, Bhūridatta the Naga King, Chaddanta the Elephant King, Prince Jayaddisa, and Prince Alīnasattu. However, specifically in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka—

“Even when being pierced by stakes and being struck by spears, I did not get angry at the hunters; this is my Perfection of Virtue.”

In this way, the Perfection of Virtue of the Bodhisatta who practiced by sacrificing his own self is called the Ultimate Perfection of Virtue (sīla-paramattha-pāramī).

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he renounced great royal majesty and fulfilled the Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī), such as in the times of Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, and Ayoghara the Wise. However, specifically in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka—

“I discarded the royal majesty that had reached my hands like a glob of spit; for me who discarded it, there was no attachment. This is my Perfection of Renunciation.”

In this way, the Perfection of Renunciation of the Bodhisatta who renounced royal majesty and went forth without attachment is called the Ultimate Perfection of Renunciation (nekkhamma-paramattha-pāramī).

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-pāramī), such as in the times of Vidhura the Wise, Mahāgovinda the Wise, Kudāla the Wise, Araka the Wise, Bodhi the Wanderer, and Mahosadha the Wise. However, specifically in the Sattubhasta Jātaka, in the time of Senaka the Wise—

“Investigating with wisdom, I released the Brahmin from suffering. There is no one equal to me in wisdom; this is my Perfection of Wisdom.”

The Perfection of Wisdom of the Bodhisatta who showed the snake inside the leather bag is called the Ultimate Perfection of Wisdom (paññā-paramattha-pāramī).

Likewise, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the Perfection of Energy (vīriya-pāramī) and others. However, specifically in the Mahājanaka Jātaka—

“In the middle of the ocean where no shore could be seen, even though all other people perished, my mind did not waver (I continued to strive); this is my Perfection of Energy.”
74:
In this way, the Perfection of Energy of the Bodhisatta who crossed the great ocean is called the Ultimate Perfection of Energy (vīriya-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Khantivādī Jātaka—
“Even though King Kāsi cut me with a sharp axe as if he were cutting a mindless log of wood, I did not get angry at him; this is my Perfection of Patience.”
In this way, the Perfection of Patience of the Bodhisatta who endured great suffering as if he were a mindless log of wood is called the Ultimate Perfection of Patience (khanti-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka—
“Protecting the word of truth and sacrificing my own life, I released one hundred and one kings from the danger of death; this is my Perfection of Truthfulness.”
In this way, the Perfection of Truthfulness of the Bodhisatta who protected the truth by sacrificing his life is called the Ultimate Perfection of Truthfulness (sacca-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Mūgapakkha Jātaka—
“It is not that my mother was not dear to me, nor was my father not dear, nor was the great fame and wealth not dear; only Omniscience (Sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) was dear to me. Therefore, I undertook the vow.”
In this way, the Perfection of Resolve of the Bodhisatta who undertook the vow by sacrificing his life is called the Ultimate Perfection of Resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-paramattha-pāramī).

In the Ekarāja Jātaka—
“At that time, no one was afraid of me, nor was I afraid of anyone. Supported by the power of loving-kindness, I delighted in the forest.”
In this way, the Perfection of Loving-kindness of the Bodhisatta who developed loving-kindness without regard for his life is called the Ultimate Perfection of Loving-kindness (mettā-paramattha-pāramī).
75:
In the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka—

“I made my bed in the cemetery, leaning against the bones of a corpse; village children came to me and showed many unseemly gestures.”

Thus, even when village children caused pleasure or pain by spitting and so forth, or by offering flowers and scents and so forth, the equanimity of one who does not overstep equanimity is called the Perfection of Equanimity in the Ultimate Sense (Upekkhā Paramattha Pāramī). This is a summary here; the detailed account should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka.

Having thus fulfilled the Perfections and remaining in the existence of King Vessantara—

“This inanimate earth, though it knows neither pleasure nor pain, yet by the power of my giving, it shook seven times.” (Cariyā. 1.124)

Having performed such great meritorious deeds as the shaking of the earth, at the end of his life, he passed away from that existence and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. There, surpassing other deities in ten respects and enjoying divine bliss, according to human calculation, when he was about to reach the end of his life within seven days, these five portents appeared: (1) his clothes became soiled, (2) his flowers withered, (3) sweat came from his armpits, (4) his body became discolored, and (5) the deity could no longer remain on his divine seat. Seeing these signs, the deities, struck with trepidation thinking, “Alas, the heavens will be empty,” and knowing the state of the Perfections fulfilled by the Great Being (Mahāsatta), thought: “This Bodhisatta, now without going to another heaven, will be born in the human world, and when he attains Buddhahood, humans who pass away after performing meritorious deeds will fill the heavens.” They then deliberated—

“When I was the divine king named Santusita in the Tusita host, the deities from the ten thousand world-systems gathered and entreated me with joined palms:

‘It is time, O Great Hero, O Divine One, to arise in a mother’s womb; delivering the world together with its deities, may you awaken to the Deathless State (Amata Pada).’” (Bu. Vaṃ. 1.66-67)
76:
Being thus entreated for the sake of becoming a Buddha (by the deities and Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems), he made his decision after making these five great observations: the time, the continent, the region, the family, and the lifespan of the mother. Passing away from that Tusita heaven, he took rebirth in the Sakyan royal family. Being nurtured there with great prosperity without decline, he gradually reached the prime of youth. In the interval, the detail should be understood by way of the sutta passages such as “Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta passed away from the Tusita host and descended into his mother’s womb” (M. Ni. 3.200) and their commentaries.

While enjoying royal splendor like the glory of the celestial realm in three palaces suitable for the three seasons, when he went out for recreation in the park, he successively saw the three divine messengers—the aged, the sick, and the dead. Struck with trepidation, he returned. On the fourth occasion, seeing a monk, he developed a preference for renunciation, thinking, “Renunciation is excellent.” He went to the park and spent the day there. While sitting by the Mangala lotus pond, he was adorned by the deity Vissakamma, who came in the guise of a barber. Having heard the news of the birth of Prince Rāhula and realizing the strength of affection for a son, he thought, “Before this bond grows, I shall cut it.” Entering the city in the evening—

“Cool (nibbutā) indeed is that mother, cool indeed is that father, cool indeed is that woman who has such a husband.”

Hearing this verse spoken by his cousin named Kisāgotamī, he thought, “This lady has made me hear the word ‘nibbuta’ (peace/extinguished) which signifies the state of peace.” He removed a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand from his neck and sent it to her. Entering his own palace and reclining on his royal couch, he saw the unseemly behavior of the sleeping dancers. With a heart filled with weariness (nibbida), he woke Channa and had him bring the horse Kanthaka. Mounting Kanthaka, with only Channa as his companion and surrounded by the deities and Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems, he departed in the Great Renunciation. In the remainder of that very night, he crossed three kingdoms and was ordained on the banks of the Anomā River. Gradually proceeding to Rājagaha, he wandered for alms in that city. While staying in the cave of Mount Paṇḍava, although invited by the King of Magadha with the offer of the kingdom, he rejected it. After he attained omniscience, the king [requested] him to visit his kingdom...
77:
The Bodhisatta, as he had promised to King Bimbisāra, approached the ascetics Āḷāra and Udaka. However, being dissatisfied with the special attainments he achieved under them, he practiced the great exertion (mahāpadhāna) for six full years. On the morning of the full moon day of Visākha, after partaking of the milk-rice offered by Sujātā at Senānigama, he floated the golden bowl in the Nerañjarā River. Having spent the daytime in various meditative attainments in the great forest grove on the banks of the Nerañjarā River, he took the eight handfuls of grass offered by Sotthiya in the evening. While being praised for his virtues by Kāla, the Nāga king, he ascended the Bodhimaṇḍa and spread the grass. He made a resolution, saying, "I shall not break this cross-legged posture as long as my mind is not liberated from the taints (āsavas) through non-clinging," and sat facing the eastern direction. Even before the sun had set, he conquered the forces of Māra. In the first watch of the night, he attained the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pubbenivāsanussatiñāṇa); in the middle watch, he attained the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings (cutūpapātañāṇa). At the end of the last watch, simultaneously with the penetration of omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa), which is adorned with all the Buddha-qualities such as the Ten Powers (dasabala) and the Four Kinds of Fearlessness (vesārajja), he realized this ocean of the Abhidhamma method. Thus, the Origin of Attainment (adhigamanidāna) of this Abhidhamma should be understood.

Note: The word "yāyanti" is spoken here according to the method of "combination of distinct capacities" (bhinnasattisamaveta). For example, when it is said, "The white one runs," it could mean a white dog running from its place, or a person of fair complexion running, or a person with a white horse running, or people wearing white clothes running. Similarly, the meaning can be understood. In the Maṇidīpa, it is also stated that "bhinnasattisamaveta" refers to the arrangement through the power of many words having distinct capacities.

Having thus realized the Abhidhamma, the Blessed One spent the week on the throne (pallaṅkasattāha), the week of the unblinking gaze (animisasattāha), and the week of the walking meditation (caṅkamanasattāha). In the fourth week, he contemplated the Abhidhamma Dhamma attained through his self-evolved knowledge (sayambhūñāṇa). Subsequently, he spent another three weeks at the Ajapāla, Mucalinda, and Rājāyatana trees. In the eighth week, while staying at the foot of the Ajapāla banyan tree, he reflected on the profundity of the Dhamma and felt inclined toward inaction, not wishing to teach. Then, Sahampati Brahma, surrounded by the hosts of Brahmas from the ten thousand world-systems, requested him to teach the Dhamma. The Blessed One surveyed the world with his Buddha-eye and, accepting the Brahma's request, looked to see, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" He then realized that Āḷāra and Udaka had passed away. Remembering the great help of the group of five monks (pañcavaggiya), he rose from his seat and traveled toward the Kāsī country. On the way, he spoke with Upaka the Ajivaka. On the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he reached the dwelling place of the group of five monks in the Deer Park at Isipatana. After convincing them—who had initially addressed him with improper terms—of his Buddhahood, he set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka). While teaching thus, he gave the ambrosia to eighteen crores of Brahmas, headed by the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. Thus, the Origin of the Teaching (desanānidāna) up to the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma should be understood. This is only a summary in this commentary. The details should be understood through the Ariyapariyesana Sutta, Pabbajja Sutta, etc., along with their commentaries.

Furthermore, the other three origins of this Abhidhamma, which is endowed with the aforementioned Adhigamanidāna and Desanānidāna—namely, the Distant Origin (dūrenidāna), the Intermediate Origin (avidūrenidāna), and the Proximate Origin (santikenidāna)—should also be known. Among them, the period from the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until reaching the Tusita heaven is known as the Distant Origin. From the Tusita heaven until reaching the Bodhimaṇḍa is known as the Intermediate Origin. The origin described by the passage, "At one time the Blessed One... was teaching the Abhidhamma discourse," is known as the Proximate Origin.
78:
The Origin of the Teaching (desanānidāna) should be understood. This is the summary here. The details, however, should be understood by way of the Ariyapariyesana Sutta, Pabbajja Sutta, and others, together with their commentaries. (In detail: The Origin of the Teaching should be understood as the events starting from the Blessed One speaking with Upaka the Ajivaka while traveling, reaching the group of five monks at the Deer Park in Isipatana on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, making them realize his Buddhahood, and teaching the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, thereby giving the ambrosia to eighteen crores of Brahmas headed by the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña.) This which has been stated is only a summary in this commentary. The details should be understood through the Ariyapariyesana Sutta, Pabbajja Sutta, etc., along with their commentaries.

Of this Abhidhamma Dhamma, which is thus endowed with the Origin of Attainment (adhigamanidāna) and the Origin of the Teaching (desanānidāna), there are three other origins: the Distant Origin (dūrenidāna), the Intermediate Origin (avidūrenidāna), and the Proximate Origin (santikenidāna). Among these three, the period from the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until reaching the Tusita heaven should be understood as the Distant Origin. From the Tusita heaven until reaching the Bodhimaṇḍa is the Intermediate Origin. This statement: "At one time the Blessed One was staying among the gods in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, at the foot of the Pāricchattaka tree on the Paṇḍukambala stone seat; there the Blessed One taught the Abhidhamma discourse to the Tāvatiṃsa gods," is the Proximate Origin of this Abhidhamma. This concludes the account of the origins (nidānakathā).

## The Account of the Origins is concluded.
79:
## 1. Cittuppādakaṇḍa
## Tikamātikāpadavaṇṇanā

Now—

“Listen with an undistracted mind to this Abhidhamma discourse that I am about to speak; for this discourse is rare to obtain.” Having promised with this verse, the opportunity to deliver the Abhidhamma discourse has arrived. In that Abhidhamma discourse, what is called ‘Abhidhamma’ consists of the seven books beginning with the Dhammasaṅgaṇī. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī also has four sections by way of the Cittuppādakaṇḍa (Section on the Arising of Consciousness), etc. The Cittuppādakaṇḍa is also twofold by way of the Mātikā (Matrix) and the Padabhājanīya (Classification of Terms). Among those two, the Mātikā is the beginning. That Mātikā is also twofold: the Tikamātikā (Matrix of Triads) and the Dukamātikā (Matrix of Dyads). Among those two, the Tikamātikā is the beginning. In the Tikamātikā, the Kusalatika (Triad of the Wholesome) is the beginning. In the Kusalatika, this term “Kusalā dhammā” is the beginning. Therefore—

“O virtuous ones, listen well with a concentrated mind to this profound Abhidhamma discourse that will be spoken starting from this term ‘Kusalā dhammā’.”

This triad, “Wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states” (Kusalā dhammā, akusalā dhammā, abyākatā dhammā), is called the Kusalatika, taking its name from the first term. This triad, “States associated with pleasant feeling, states associated with painful feeling, states associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling” (Sukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā, dukkhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā, adukkhamasukhāya vedanāya sampayuttā dhammā), is called the Vedanātika, taking its name from all its terms. In this way, the names of all triads and dyads should be understood either by way of the first term or by way of all terms. All of these are established by fifteen divisions. There is one division for the triads and fourteen for the dyads. The six dyads beginning with “States that are roots, states that are not roots” (Hetū dhammā, nahetū dhammā) are called the “Hetugocchaka” (Cluster of Roots) because they stand connected to each other in terms of text and meaning, like a pinnacle or like a cluster [of pots]. Apart from that, the seven dyads beginning with “States with conditions, states without conditions” (Sappaccayā dhammā, appaccayā dhammā) should be known as the “Cūḷantaraduka” (Lesser Intermediate Dyads) because they are not connected to each other but are selected and placed in between the clusters simply due to the commonality of being dyads, and because they are smaller than the other Mahantaraduka (Greater Dyads). After that, by way of the six beginning with the Āsavaduka...
80:
“Āsavagocchaka” (Cluster of Taints); similarly, by way of the Saṃyojanaduka (Dyad of Fetters), etc., it is the “Saṃyojanagocchaka” (Cluster of Fetters); similarly, by way of the Ganthaduka, Oghaduka, Yogaduka, and Nīvaraṇaduka, etc., they are the “Ganthagocchaka, Oghagocchaka, Yogagocchaka, and Nīvaraṇagocchaka.” By way of the five dyads beginning with the Parāmāsaduka, it is known as the “Parāmāsagocchaka.” All seven clusters (gocchaka) should be known. After that, the fourteen dyads beginning with “States with an object” (Sārammaṇā dhammā) are called the “Mahantaraduka” (Greater Dyads). After that, the six dyads beginning with the Upādānaduka are called the “Upādānagocchaka” (Cluster of Clinging). After that, the eight dyads beginning with the Kilesaduka are called the “Kilesagocchaka” (Cluster of Defilements). After that, the eighteen dyads beginning with the Dassanenapahātabbaduka are called the “Piṭṭhiduka” (End Dyads) because they are placed at the end of the Abhidhamma Matrix. Specifically, the forty-two dyads beginning with “States partaking of clear vision, states partaking of ignorance” (Vijjābhāgino dhammā, avijjābhāgino dhammā) are called the “Suttantikaduka” (Suttanta Dyads). Thus, all these triads and dyads should be known as being established by fifteen divisions.

These triads and dyads thus established are of two groups by way of Sappadesa (with remainder) and Nippadesa (without remainder). Among them, nine triads and seventy-one dyads are called “Sappadesa” because they encompass the material and immaterial states that have remaining portions. The remaining thirteen triads and seventy-one dyads are called “Nippadesa.” Among those Sappadesa and Nippadesa, first, among the triads, these nine triads are called “Sappadesa”: the Vedanātika, Vitakkatika, Pītitika, Uppannatika, Atītatika, and the four Ārammaṇatikas. Among the dyads, these seventy-one dyads are called “Sappadesa”: the three dyads at the end of each of the nine clusters ending with the Upādānagocchaka, the four dyads at the end of the Kilesagocchaka, the two Mahantaradukas “States associated with consciousness, states dissociated from consciousness” and “States conjoined with consciousness, states not conjoined with consciousness,” and the remaining thirty-eight dyads excluding these four dyads among the Suttantikadukas: the Adhivacanaduka, Niruttiduka, Paññattiduka, and Nāmarūpaduka. All the other triads and dyads besides those mentioned should be known as “Nippadesa.”

Now, this is the sequential explanation of the terms of the Matrix beginning with “Kusalā dhammā.” First, the word ‘kusala’ is seen in the senses of health (ārogya), faultlessness (anavajja), skill (cheka), and happy result (sukhavipāka). This word ‘kusala’ is seen in the sense of health (ārogya) in such passages as: “Is the venerable one healthy (kusala)? Is the venerable one free from illness?” In the sense of faultlessness (anavajja), it is seen in: “Venerable sir, what kind of bodily conduct is wholesome (kusala)? Great King, whatever bodily conduct is faultless (anavajja), that bodily conduct is wholesome.” And also: “Venerable sir, there is yet another excellent state...” [seen in the sense of faultlessness].
81:
## 
In sentences such as “The Blessed One teaches the Dhamma in such a way; in those blameless (wholesome) states taught, the Blessed One is supreme” (from the Sampasādanīya Sutta of the Pāthika Vagga, Dīgha Nikāya), the word *kusala* is used in the sense of blamelessness (*anavajja*). In sentences such as “You are skillful (*kusalo*) in the various parts of a chariot” and “Women who are skillful (*kusalā*) in dancing and singing, well-trained and graceful (will delight you),” the word *kusala* is used in the sense of skillfulness (*cheka*). In sentences such as “Monks, due to the cause of undertaking wholesome states (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*), (this merit increases)” and “Because wholesome karma (*kusalassa kammassa*) has been performed and accumulated, (eye-consciousness arises),” the word *kusala* is used in the sense of having a happy result (*sukhavipāka*). In this context (of the phrase *kusalā dhammā*), the word *kusala* carries the meanings of health (*ārogya*), blamelessness (*anavajja*), and happy result (*sukhavipāka*).

The word *dhamma* is found in the senses of scriptural learning (*pariyatti*), cause (*hetu*), quality or virtue (*guṇa*), and the state of being non-self and non-soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*), etc. This word *dhamma* is found in the sense of scriptural learning in sentences such as “He learns the Dhamma (the scriptures), the Suttas, and the Geyyas.” It is found in the sense of cause (*hetu*) in sentences such as “Knowledge of the cause is the discrimination of Dhamma (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).”

“Wholesome states and unwholesome states,
Do not both have equal results;
Unwholesome states lead to hell,
Wholesome states lead to a good destination.”

In such verses, it is found in the sense of quality or virtue (*guṇa*). In sentences such as “At that time, there are dhammas” and “He dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas,” it is found in the sense of being non-self and non-soul (*nissatta-nijjīvatā*). In this context as well, the word *dhamma* refers only to the state of being non-self and non-soul.

The etymological definition (*vacanattha*) in this context is as follows: They are called wholesome (*kusalā*) because they shake, destroy, and shatter contemptible, evil states. Alternatively, they are called *kusa* because they exist in a contemptible manner (within the continuity of beings). They are called wholesome (*kusalā*) because they cut (*lunanti*) those *kusa* known as the unwholesome. Alternatively, wisdom is called *kusa* because it makes contemptible unwholesome states thin or brings them to an end. They are called wholesome (*kusalā*) because they should be taken up or practiced (*lātabbā*) by that *kusa* (wisdom); this means they are to be acquired or developed. Alternatively, just as *kusa* grass cuts the hand on both sides, these states also cut the group of defilements on both sides—those that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen. Therefore, they are called *kusalā* because they cut like *kusa* grass. They are called *dhammā* because they bear (*dhārenti*) their own intrinsic nature. Alternatively, they are called *dhammā* because they are borne by conditions, or because they are understood according to their intrinsic nature. Those that are not wholesome are unwholesome (*akusalā*). Just as the opposite of a friend is called an enemy (*amitta*), or the opposites of greed, etc., are called non-greed, etc., it means states that are the opposite of the wholesome. They are called indeterminate (*abyākata*) because they are not declared (as wholesome or unwholesome). It means states that are not spoken of as being wholesome or unwholesome. Among those (wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states)—
82:
## 
Furthermore, states characterized by blamelessness and happy results are wholesome (*kusalā*). States characterized by faultiness and painful results are unwholesome (*akusalā*). States characterized by the absence of result are indeterminate (*abyākata*).

Do these terms such as '*kusalā*' and '*dhammā*' have the same meaning or different meanings? What is the point here? If they have the same meaning, then the phrase '*kusalā dhammā*' would be the same as saying '*kusalā kusalā*'. If they have different meanings, then the triads (*tika*) would become groups of six (*chakka*) and the dyads (*duka*) would become groups of four (*catukka*), and there would be no connection between the words.

Indeed, just as when one says '*kusalā*', '*rūpaṃ*', '*cakkhumā*', there is no connection between the words as they do not regard each other in terms of meaning, so too in this case, there would be a lack of connection between the words. Words devoid of preceding and succeeding connection are indeed useless. Furthermore, it would contradict the subsequent question: “Which states are wholesome?” (*katame dhammā kusalā?*). If the *dhammas* were not wholesome, then it is said: “Which states are wholesome?” Another way: If these words had the same meaning, because the three '*dhammā*' words have the same meaning, the meanings of 'wholesome', etc., would also become one. For the three '*dhammā*' words following 'wholesome', etc., are identical in their nature as *dhamma*. Therefore, 'wholesome', etc., which are not different in meaning from the three *dhammas*, would also become identical. [It would mean:] “Whatever is wholesome is unwholesome, and that is indeterminate.” [The objector continues:] “Even if you do not accept that the three *dhammas* are identical, and say that the *dhamma* following 'wholesome' is one thing, the *dhamma* following 'unwholesome' is another, and the *dhamma* following 'indeterminate' is yet another; if this were so, *dhamma* is a reality (*bhāva*), and that which is other than reality is non-reality (*abhāva* or concept). Therefore, the *dhamma* following 'unwholesome' would be a non-reality, being different from the *dhamma* called reality following 'wholesome'. Likewise, the *dhamma* following 'indeterminate' would be a non-reality. And the *dhamma* following 'wholesome' would also be different from them. Thus, 'wholesome', etc., which are not different from these *dhammas* that have become non-realities, would themselves be non-realities (concepts).”

All this is without reason. Why? Because the establishment of usage (*vohāra*) is according to convention. Indeed, usage is established in whatever way it is agreed upon and accepted regarding meanings. In sentences such as '*kusalā dhammā*', the expression '*dhamma*' preceded by 'wholesome' and the expression 'wholesome' followed by '*dhamma*' are not accepted by the wise as having no distinction in meaning, as in the case of saying '*kusalā kusalā*'. Nor are they accepted as having meanings that do not regard each other, like the words '*kusalā*', '*rūpaṃ*', and '*cakkhumā*'. In this context, the word '*kusala*' refers to what is called blamelessness and happy result...
83:
The word 'kusala' is accepted by the wise as illuminating the meaning of being faultless and having happy results; the word 'akusala' as illuminating the meaning of being blameworthy and having painful results; the word 'abyākata' as illuminating the meaning of being without result; and the word 'dhamma' as illuminating the meaning of bearing its own nature and so forth. When this word 'dhamma' is spoken immediately after any one of these [kusala, akusala, or abyākata], it indicates its general meaning (sāmaññattha). This is because all these—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—are called 'dhamma' by the characteristic of bearing their own nature and so forth.

The words such as 'kusala' spoken before the word 'dhamma' also indicate their specific meaning (visesattha) to that word 'dhamma'. Indeed, a dhamma is either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. Thus, when these words are spoken individually, they are accepted by the wise as illuminating only their respective meanings. Even when spoken together with the word 'dhamma', they are accepted by the wise in the world as illuminating their general meaning or their specific meaning. Therefore, whatever is stated here as a reason for reproach by speculating on the identity or difference of meanings is without logical ground. This is the sequential explanation of the terms of the Wholesome Triad (Kusala-tika). In this same manner, the method for the remaining triads and dyads should also be understood. Hereafter, I shall speak only of the specific meanings.

In the phrases such as "sukhāya vedanāya" (with pleasant feeling), the word 'sukha' is first seen in the meanings of pleasant feeling, the root of happiness, the object of happiness, the proximate cause of happiness, the supportive place of happiness, peace, and Nibbāna. This word 'sukha' appears in the sense of pleasant feeling in such passages as "sukhassa ca pahānā" (with the abandoning of pleasure). It appears in the sense of the root of happiness (remote cause) in such passages as "sukho buddhānaṃ uppādo" (happy is the arising of the Buddhas) and "sukhā virāgatā loke" (detachment is happy in the world). It appears in the sense of the object of happiness in such passages as "Yasmā ca kho, Mahāli, rūpaṃ sukhaṃ sukhānupatitaṃ sukhāvakkantaṃ" (Because, Mahāli, form is pleasant, followed by pleasure, and entered by pleasure). It appears in the sense of the cause of happiness (proximate cause) in such passages as "Sukhassetaṃ, bhikkhave, adhivacanaṃ yadidaṃ puññāni" (Bhikkhus, this is a designation for happiness, that is, merit). It appears in the sense of the supportive place of happiness in such passages as "Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva sukhā saggā" (Bhikkhus, it is not easy to reach the end by description as to how happy the heavens are) and "Na te sukhaṃ pajānanti ye na passanti nandanaṃ" (They do not know happiness who do not see the Nandana grove). It appears in the sense of peace (freedom from affliction) in such passages as "Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārā ete dhammā" (These states are dwellings in happiness in the present life). It appears in the sense of Nibbāna in such passages as "Nibbānaṃ paramaṃ sukhaṃ" (Nibbāna is the highest happiness). Here, however, this word 'sukha' should be understood as pleasant feeling only. The word 'vedanā' occurs only in the sense of experiencing (vedayita) in such passages as "Viditā vedanā uppajjanti" (Known feelings arise).
84:
The word 'dukkha' is seen in the meanings of painful feeling, the basis of suffering (dukkha-vatthu), the object of suffering (dukkhārammaṇa), the cause of suffering (dukkha-paccaya), and the supportive place of suffering (dukkha-paccayatthāna), etc. This word 'dukkha' is evident in the sense of painful feeling in such sentences as "dukkhassa ca pahānā" (with the abandoning of pain). It is evident in the sense of the basis of suffering in such sentences as "jātipi dukkhā" (birth also is suffering). It is evident in the sense of the object of suffering in such sentences as "Yasmā ca kho, Mahāli, rūpaṃ dukkhaṃ dukkhānupatitaṃ dukkhāvakkantaṃ" (Because, Mahāli, form is suffering, followed by suffering, and entered by suffering). It is evident in the sense of the cause of suffering in such sentences as "dukkho pāpassa uccayo" (the accumulation of evil is suffering). It is evident in the sense of the supportive place of suffering in such sentences as "Yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, na sukaraṃ akkhānena pāpuṇituṃ yāva dukkhā nirayā" (Bhikkhus, it is not easy to reach the end by description as to how painful the hells are). Here, however, that word 'dukkha' should be understood only in the sense of painful feeling.

As for the etymology (vacanattha) here: It is 'sukha' because it pleases (sukhayati). It is 'dukkha' because it pains (dukkhayati). It is 'adukkhamasukha' because it is neither painful nor pleasant. The letter 'm' is stated by way of euphonic junction (padasandhi). All feelings are called 'vedanā' because they feel or experience the flavor of the object. Among those feelings, the feeling characterized by experiencing a desirable object is called 'sukha'. The feeling characterized by experiencing an undesirable object is called 'dukkha'. The feeling characterized by experiencing an object that is the opposite of both (a neutral object) is called 'adukkhamasukha'. The meaning of the word 'sampayutta' (associated) which is present in all these three terms is: they are 'sampayutta' because they are associated by way of equal modes. By what kind of modes are they associated? They are associated by way of having the same arising (ekuppādatā), etc. Indeed, in rejecting the question, "Are there no states associated with any states? Yes [there are]," the meaning of association (sampayoga) was taught by way of having the same arising, etc., thus: "Are there not some states that are co-existent (sahagata), co-nascent (sahajāta), conjoined (saṃsaṭṭha), having the same arising (ekuppāda), having the same cessation (ekanirodha), having the same base (ekavatthuka), and having the same object (ekārammaṇa) with some other states?" Thus, they are called 'sampayutta' because they are associated by way of these equal modes such as having the same arising.

In the Result Triad (Vipāka-tika), they are called 'vipāka' (results) because they are the results of wholesome and unwholesome states which are distinct from one another. This is a designation for mental states (arūpa-dhamma) that have reached the state of being a result. 'Vipākadhamma-dhammā' means states that have the nature of result. Just as beings who have the nature of birth and decay, or whose character is birth and decay, are called 'jātidhamma' and 'jarādhamma', so too, states that have the nature of result or the character of result in the sense of producing a result are meant by 'vipākadhamma'. The third term [of the triad] is stated by way of rejecting both natures.

In the Clung-to and Favorable to Clinging Triad (Upādinnupādāniya-tika), they are called 'upādinna' (clung-to) because they are taken up as results by kamma which is associated with craving and views by way of making them objects.
85:
States that are beneficial to the graspings (upādāna) because they have become objects and are connected with grasping are called upādāniya (subject to grasping). This is a designation for states that serve as the object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) for grasping. Because these states are both clung to (by kamma) and are objects of grasping, they are called upādiṇṇupādāniya (clung-to and subject to grasping). This is a designation for mental and material states produced by kamma that are objects of the taints (āsava). In this same manner, the meaning in the remaining two terms should be understood along with the negation (paṭisedha).

In the triad of the defiled and the provocative of defilement (saṅkiliṭṭha-saṅkilesika-tika), it is called saṅkilesa (defilement) because it oppresses and causes torment. It means it oppresses and torments. States associated with defilement are called saṅkiliṭṭha (defiled). They are called saṅkilesika (provocative of defilement) either because they deserve defilement by occurring with themselves as the object, or because they do not transcend being the object of defilement. This is a designation for states that are the object-condition for defilement. States that are both defiled and provocative of defilement are called saṅkiliṭṭha-saṅkilesika. The remaining two terms should be understood in the same way as mentioned in the previous triad.

In the triad of initial thought (vitakka), states that occur together with initial thought by way of association are called savitakka (with initial thought). States that occur together with sustained thought (vicāra) are called savicāra (with sustained thought). States that occur with both initial and sustained thought are called savitakka-savicāra. States devoid of both are called avitakka-avicāra. Among initial and sustained thought, states that have only sustained thought as their measure (pamāṇa) are called vicāramatta. It means they do not reach association with initial thought beyond sustained thought. States that have only sustained thought as their measure without initial thought are called avitakka-vicāramatta.

In the triad of rapture (pīti), states that have reached the state of arising together with rapture are called pītisahagata (accompanied by rapture); this means they are associated with rapture. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. Here, upekkhā (equanimity) refers to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (adukkhamasukha-vedanā). That feeling is called equanimity because it disregards the modes of pleasure and pain and remains in a neutral mode. Thus, by taking two terms from the triad of feeling, this triad is taught by way of showing the distinction of pleasure without rapture from pleasure with rapture.

In the triad of vision (dassana), vision refers to the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga). That path is taught as vision because it sees Nibbāna for the first time. Although the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) sees it first, for example, a person who comes to the king for some business might see the king on an elephant in the street from afar, yet [when asked] 'Have you seen...
86:
...the king?', he says 'I have not seen him' because his business is not yet completed, even though he has seen him. Similarly, although [the change-of-lineage knowledge] sees Nibbāna, it is not called 'vision' because the task of abandoning the defilements has not yet been accomplished. In truth, that knowledge stands only in the position of adverting (āvajjana) to the path. The remaining three paths are called 'development' (bhāvanā). This is because the remaining three paths arise by way of development only in the truths already seen by the first path; they do not see anything new not seen before. Therefore, they are called 'development'. The third term is taught by way of the negation of both.

In the triad immediately following that triad of vision, 'states having roots to be abandoned by vision' means that the roots of those states are abandoned by the path of stream-entry. The second term should be understood in the same way. In the third term, the meaning should be taken as 'the roots to be abandoned by vision or by development do not exist for those states'. Otherwise, if the meaning were taken as 'the roots are not abandoned', it would result in not including rootless (ahetuka) states, because in rootless states, there is no root at all to be abandoned by vision or development. Also, in states with roots (sahetuka), it would lead to the abandoning of states other than the roots, but not the roots themselves; for it is only the roots of those states with roots that are taught as 'not to be abandoned by vision or development', not the states themselves. Neither of these two meanings is intended. Therefore, only the meaning 'the roots to be abandoned by vision or by development do not exist for those states' should be taken.

In the triad of leading to accumulation (ācayagāmi), it is called ācaya (accumulation) because it is increased by kamma and defilements. This is a name for rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), decease (cuti), destination (gati), and the round of existence (vaṭṭa). They are called ācayagāmi because they are the cause and producer of that accumulation, or because they lead that person to the aforementioned accumulation. This is a designation for wholesome and unwholesome states that are objects of the taints. Because it is devoid of the round of existence called accumulation, Nibbāna is called apacaya (diminution). States that lead to diminution because they occur with Nibbāna as their object are called apacayagāmi; this is a designation for the noble paths (ariya-magga). Alternatively, they are called ācayagāmi because they go about building up the round of existence, just as a mason builds a wall. They are called apacayagāmi because they go about dismantling that very round of existence, like a man destroying the bricks laid by that mason. The third term is taught by the negation of both.

In the triad of the trainee (sekha), they are called sekha because they are born in the three trainings (sikkhā). They are also called sekha because they belong to the seven types of trainees. They are also called sekha because, their training being incomplete, they are training themselves.
87:
Sekkha states. Because there is nothing further to be learned or practiced above, they are not Sekkha, thus they are called Asekkha. Alternatively, they are called Asekkha because they possess training (sikkhā) that has reached growth. This is a designation for the states of the fruition of Arahantship (arahattaphala). The third term is stated by way of excluding both.

In the Paritta triad, because it is limited on all sides, a small object is called 'paritta', as in 'parittaṃ gomayapiṇḍaṃ' (a small lump of cow dung), etc. These sense-sphere states are also like paritta because of their small power; therefore, they are called paritta. This is a designation for sense-sphere states (kāmāvacara-dhamma). States that have reached greatness because of their ability to suppress defilements, their extensive results, and their long duration are called mahaggata. Alternatively, they are called mahaggata because they are practiced by persons possessing noble desire, energy, consciousness, and wisdom. Defilements such as greed, which make measurements, are called 'pamāṇa' (measure). Because these states have no measure either by way of object or by way of association, and because they are the opposite of measure, they are called appamāṇa.

In the Parittārammaṇa triad, states that have a limited (sense-sphere) object are called parittārammaṇa. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

In the Hīna triad, low, unwholesome states are called hīna. The remaining states of the three planes that exist in the middle of the inferior and the superior are called majjhima. Supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma) are called paṇīta because of their noble meaning and because of the sense of being insatiable (due to excellence).

In the Micchatta triad, although they are desired with the thought 'these will bring me benefit and happiness', they are called micchatta (wrongness) because they do not turn out that way, and because they occur pervertedly, such as seeing beauty in the foul, etc. They are called niyata (fixed) because, when there is the giving of a result, they give the result immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates. Because they are both wrong and fixed, they are called micchattaniyata. States that have a right nature, in the sense opposite to what was stated, are called sammatta. Because they are both right and fixed by giving their fruit immediately after themselves, they are called sammattaniyata. States that are not fixed in either way are called aniyata.

In the Maggārammaṇa triad, it is called Magga (Path) because it seeks Nibbāna, or because it goes along killing the defilements. States that have the Path as an object are called maggārammaṇa. The eightfold Path is called maggahētuka because it is a cause by way of the path-condition (magga-paccaya). Alternatively, the roots (hētus) associated with the Path, or the roots existing in the Path, are called magga-hētus. These roots are for these states...
88:
...causes, thus they are also called maggahētuka. Right View (sammādiṭṭhi) is itself both the Path and a root. Thus, because the Path is the root for these states, they are also called maggahētuka. Because of the sense of occurring by way of overcoming, the Path is the predominant factor (adhipati) for these states; thus they are called maggādhipati.

In the Uppanna triad, states that have occurred and are proceeding upwards from arising (uppāda) until dissolution (bhaṅga) are called uppanna (arisen). Those that have not arisen are called anuppanna. States that will definitely arise because a portion of their completed causes exists are called uppādino.

In the Atīta triad, states that have reached and passed beyond their own nature or the moment of arising, etc., are called atīta (past). States that have not yet reached either of those two stages are called anāgata (future). States that are arising depending on their respective causes are called paccuppanna (present).

In the Anantara triad, states that have a past object are called atītārammaṇa. The same method applies to the remaining two terms.

In the Ajjhatta triad, states that occur based on the self (attabhāva) with the intention of reaching the assumption that 'we, occurring in this way, are the self' are called ajjhatta (internal). This word 'ajjhatta' is found in four meanings: gocarajjhatta, niyakajjhatta, ajjhattajjhatta, and visayajjhatta. In passages such as 'Ānanda, that bhikkhu should settle his mind internally (ajjhattaṃ) only on that same previous sign of concentration' and 'delighting in the internal (ajjhatta), concentrated', the meaning of gocarajjhatta is found. In passages such as 'internal (ajjhatta) clarity' and 'he dwells contemplating dhammas in dhammas internally (ajjhatta)', the meaning of niyakajjhatta is found. In passages such as 'six internal (ajjhattika) bases', the meaning of ajjhattajjhatta is found. In passages such as 'Ānanda, this dwelling has been fully realized by the Tathāgata, namely, by not attending to any signs, he enters and dwells in internal (ajjhatta) emptiness', the meaning of visayajjhatta is found. Here, visayajjhatta means the sphere of mastery (issariyaṭṭhāna). Indeed, the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) is called the sphere of mastery for the Buddhas.

In this context, however, niyakajjhatta is intended. Therefore, states belonging to individual persons occurring within their own continuity are to be known as ajjhatta. Those that are external to that, whether bound to the sense-faculties or not, are called bahiddha (external). The third term is stated by way of both.
89:
The Anantara-tika (Ajjhatta-bahiddha-tika) is taught by way of arising with those three types of phenomena—internal, external, and internal-external—as objects.

In the Sanidassana-tika, states that are with visibility, known as the state of being seen, are called 'sanidassana'. States that are with impingement, known as the state of being struck or striking, are called 'sappaṭigha'. States that are both visible and with impingement are called 'sanidassana-sappaṭigha'. Because those states do not have visibility, known as the state of being seen, they are called 'anidassana'. States that do not have visibility but are with impingement in the manner already stated are called 'anidassana-sappaṭigha'. The third term is taught by way of negating both. This is the sequential commentary (vaṇṇanā) on the terms in the Tika-mātikā.

## The Commentary on the Terms of the Tika-mātikā is Finished.

## Commentary on the Terms of the Duka-mātikā

1–6. In the Duka-mātikā, however, I shall only provide the commentary on the terms not yet explained in the Triads. In the Hetu-gocchaka, first, 'hetu-dhammā' refers to states called roots (hetu) in the sense of being a foundation (mūla). There is also a reading 'hetū dhammā'. The phrase 'na hetū' is a statement negating those very roots. States that arise together with a root by way of association (sampayoga) are called 'sahetuka'. States that arise in such a way but without a root are called 'ahetuka'. States associated with a root because of having a common arising (ekuppāda), etc., are called 'hetu-sampayutta'. States not associated with a root are called 'hetu-vippayutta'. Although there is no difference in meaning between these two couplets, they are taught either by way of the elegance of the teaching (desanā-vilāsa) or by way of the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those persons who can understand in that way. Furthermore, by combining the first couplet with the second and third, three other couplets are also taught according to possibility, by way of terms such as 'hetū na hetū', etc. In that text, just as the couplet term 'hetū ceva dhammā sahetukā ca' is possible, so too is this couplet term 'hetū ceva dhammā ahetukā ca'. And just as the couplet term 'sahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū' is possible, so too is this couplet term 'ahetukā ceva dhammā na ca hetū'. The same method should be understood in the combination with the hetu-sampayutta couplet.

In that text, although 'na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi' is complete, the additional phrase 'kho pana' is stated in 'na hetū khေါ pana dhammā'. By the power of that (phrase 'kho pana'), the following additional meaning is included. How should it be understood? It is not that only the non-root states (na-hetu-dhamma) occur as sahetuka and ahetuka; in fact, other root states (hetu-dhamma) also occur as sahetuka and ahetuka. It is not that only the non-root states occur as sahetuka and ahetuka; in fact, they also occur by way of the other divisions of hetu-sampayutta and hetu-vippayutta.
90:
By the power of [the phrase 'kho pana'], it should be understood that this additional meaning is included. How? Not only 'na hetū dhammā', but indeed others also, and not only 'sahetukāpi ahetukāpi', but indeed in other ways too. This is what is meant: Just as 'na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi', so too 'hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi'. And just as 'na hetū dhammā sahetukāpi ahetukāpi', so too it should be understood that 'na hetū dhammā hetu-sampayuttāpi hetu-vippayuttāpi'.

7–13. In the Cūḷantara-dukas (Lesser Intermediate Couplets), states are called 'sappaccaya' because they occur together with the causes (paccaya) that produce them. They are called 'appaccaya' because there is no cause for their arising or persistence. They are called 'saṅkhata' because they are made by the meeting of conditions. They are called 'asaṅkhata' because they are not conditioned by causes. They are called 'rūpī' because they have form (rūpa), such as the earth element, etc., by way of inseparability. They are called 'arūpī' because they do not have such form. Or, they are called 'rūpī' because they have the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana). If not so, they are 'arūpī'. The round of existence (vaṭṭa) is called 'loka' (world) because of its nature of disintegrating; states are called 'lokiya' (mundane) because they are associated with the world by being included within that round. They are called 'uttara' because they have emerged from that world; they are called 'lokuttara' (supramundane) because they have emerged from the world by not being included in the world. They are called 'kenaci viññeyya' (cognizable by some) because they are to be known by any one of the consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, etc. They are called 'kenaci na viññeyya' because they are not to be known by those very consciousnesses such as eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, etc. Thus, because of the difference in meaning, the two terms form a couplet.

14–19. In the Āsava-gocchaka (Taint Cluster), they are called 'āsava' (taints) because they flow out. This means they flow or occur from the eye-door up to the mind-door. Or, they are called 'āsava' because they flow, in terms of states, up to the gotrabhū stage, and in terms of space (okāsa), up to the peak of existence (bhavagga). The meaning is that they occur by encompassing these states and this space. This 'ā' syllable has the meaning of encompassing. Just as fermented liquors such as spirits are called 'āsava' in the sense of being long-matured, these are also called 'āsava' because they are like those liquors. In the world, long-matured spirits, etc., are called 'āsava' are spoken of. If they are called 'āsava' in the sense of being long-matured, then only these defilements deserve to be 'āsava'. For it has been said: 'Monks, a beginning point of ignorance is not known, such that before this, ignorance did not exist,' etc. Or, they are called 'āsava' because they flow or produce the long suffering of saṃsāra. States other than those taints are called 'no-āsava'. They are called 'sāsava' because they occur together with the taints that arise taking them as objects. They are called 'anāsava' because they do not have such taints that arise taking them as objects. The remaining words should be understood in the same way as stated in the Hetu-duka. As for the distinction...
91: States that occur together with taints (āsava) are called sāsava (with taints). States in which taints do not occur by taking them as an object are called anāsava (without taints). The rest should be understood in the manner stated in the Hetugocchaka (Cluster of Roots). This is the distinction: in that Hetugocchaka, the final dyad, 'States that are not roots but are associated with roots or are rootless,' was taught by placing the second term of the first dyad at the beginning; however, in this Āsavagocchaka, it is not taught as 'States that are not taints but are with taints or are without taints.' Even if it is not so taught, this dyad and other varieties of dyads should be understood in the same manner as stated in that cluster.## 20-25. In the Saṃyojanagocchaka (Cluster of Fetters): those states that exist for a person and bind or tie that person in the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) are called saṃyojana (fetters). Other states are called 'not fetters' (no saṃyojana). States that are beneficial to fetters by becoming their objects and being connected with them are called saṃyojaniya (subject to fetters). This is a designation for states that are objects of fetters. States that are not subject to fetters are called asaṃyojaniya. The rest should be applied in the manner stated in the Hetugocchaka.## 26-31. In the Ganthagocchaka (Cluster of Ties): those states that exist for a person and tie or join that person in the round by way of death and rebirth are called gantha (ties). Other states are called 'not ties' (no gantha). States that are to be tied by ties by way of making them an object are called ganthaniya (subject to ties). The rest should be applied in the manner stated in the Hetugocchaka. Just as it is understood here, in the subsequent clusters, the remaining statements should be understood in the manner stated in each respective cluster.## 32-37. In the Oghagocchaka (Cluster of Floods): those states that exist for a person and cause that person to sink or submerge in the round are called ogha (floods). States that are to be overwhelmed by floods because they are overwhelmed after being made an object are called oghaniya (subject to floods). Only states that are objects of floods should be known as oghaniya.## 38-43. In the Yogagocchaka (Cluster of Yokes): they are called yoga (yokes) because they yoke [beings] to the round. Yoganiya states should be understood like oghaniya states.## 44-49. In the Nīvaraṇagocchaka (Cluster of Hindrances): they are called nīvaraṇa (hindrances) because they obstruct or shroud the mind. Nīvaraṇiya states should be understood like saṃyojaniya states.
92:
50-54. In the Parāmāsa-gocchaka (Cluster of Misapprehensions): Because they misapprehend by surpassing the true nature of things, such as impermanence, and adhering to them as 'permanent' etc., they are called 'Parāmāsa' (misapprehensions). Because they are misapprehended by those misapprehensions through the power of making them objects, they are called 'Parāmaṭṭha' (misapprehended).

55-68. In the Mahantara-dukas (Intermediate Dyads): Because they cannot arise without taking an object, the states that occur with an object are called 'Sārammaṇa'. The states that have no object are called 'Anārammaṇa'. It is called 'Citta' (consciousness) because it cognizes the object, or because it is variegated. Because they are associated with consciousness without separation, they are called 'Cetasika' (mental factors). Because they are continuously conjoined with consciousness from their arising until their cessation, they are called 'Cittasaṃsaṭṭha' (conjoined with consciousness). Although they arise together with consciousness, because they are not continuously conjoined, they are called 'Cittavisaṃsaṭṭha' (not conjoined with consciousness). That which has consciousness as its cause of arising is called 'Cittasamuṭṭhāna' (produced by consciousness). States that arise together are called 'Sahabhū'. States that arise together with consciousness are called 'Cittasahabhū'. States that arise following the sequence of consciousness are called 'Cittānuparivatti'. States that are both conjoined with consciousness and produced by consciousness are called 'Cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhāna'. States that are endowed with all three—conjoined with consciousness, produced by consciousness, and arising together with consciousness—are called 'Cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānasahabhū'. States that are endowed with all three—conjoined with consciousness, produced by consciousness, and following the sequence of consciousness—are called 'Cittasaṃsaṭṭhasamuṭṭhānānuparivatti'. All remaining terms should be understood by the power of the opposite of the terms already mentioned. As stated in the Ajjhatta-ttika (Triad of the Internal), the six internal bases (ajjhattikāyatana) occurring within one's own continuity are called 'Ajjhattika' (internal). States external to that are called 'Bāhira' (external). Because they arise depending on the great essentials (mahābhūta), they are called 'Upādā' (derived). States that are not so are called 'No-upādā'.

69-74. In the Upādāna-gocchaka (Cluster of Clinging): Because they cling strongly, they are called 'Upādāna' (clinging). It means a firm grasping. States other than those are called 'No-upādāna'.

75-82. In the Kilesa-gocchaka (Cluster of Defilements): The meaning should be understood in the same way as stated in the Saṃkiliṭṭha-ttika (Triad of the Defiled).

83-100. In the Piṭṭhi-dukas (Concluding Dyads): Because they frequent the sense sphere, they are called 'Kāmāvacara' (of the sense sphere), because they frequent the fine-material sphere, they are called 'Rūpāvacara' (of the fine-material sphere), and because they frequent the immaterial sphere, they are called 'Arūpāvacara' (of the immaterial sphere). This is only a summary here. The detailed explanation will be made clear later. Because they are included within the round of existence of the three planes, they are called 'Pariyāpanna' (included). States not included in that round are called 'Apariyāpanna' (unincluded). Because they cut the root of the round of existence and, taking Nibbāna as the object, lead out from the suffering of the round, they are called 'Niyyānika' (emancipatory).
93:
Because they do not lead out from the suffering of the round of rebirth by this characteristic, they are called aniyyānika. Because they are certain to give results either immediately after death or immediately after their own occurrence, they are called niyata. Because they are not certain in giving results in that way, they are called aniyata. Because they can abandon states other than themselves, they are called uttara. Because they occur together with states that are capable of transcending them, they are called sauttara. Because there are no states capable of transcending them, they are called anuttara. Beings lament because of these states; therefore, they are called raṇa. Beings oppressed by lust and so on lament in various ways; thus, raṇa is a designation for that lust and so on. Because they occur together with states like lust that cause lamentation, through the power of association or by being established in a single person as things to be abandoned, they are called saraṇa.
