While searching for the ox, he climbed Uttaravaḍḑhamāna Mountain. There, a large python caught and coiled around him. He thought, "I will cut off the snake's head with this sharp billhook." Then he thought again, "It is not proper for me to break the precepts I have taken from my venerable teacher." Having thought this up to three times, he decided, "I will sacrifice only my life, but I will not sacrifice the precepts," and threw the sharp billhook on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the python released the Upāsaka and went away. Abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati) should be understood as the abstinence associated with the Noble Path (ariya-magga). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the mere thought "I will kill a living being" no longer occurs to the Noble Ones (ariya-puggala). Just as the analysis (vinicchaya) of the ten unwholesome courses of action was understood by five aspects, so should the analysis of these ten wholesome courses of action be understood by five aspects: Dhamma, portion (koṭṭhāsa), object (ārammaṇa), feeling (vedanā), and root (mūla). Among these, the analysis by way of Dhamma is: among these ten wholesome courses of action, the first seven in order can be both volition (cetanā) and abstinence (virati). The last three are only mental factors associated with volition. By way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), the first seven in order are called "courses of action" (kammapatha). The roots are...
147:
Thinking, "I will sacrifice my life, but I will not sacrifice the precept," he threw the sharp bone-handled axe that was on his shoulder into the forest. At that very moment, the great python released that lay devotee and went away.

Abstinence associated with the Noble Path should be known as 'abstinence by eradication' (samuccheda-virati). From the moment that abstinence arises, even the slightest thought of "I will kill a living being" does not arise in Noble Persons (ariya-puggala).

Now, just as the analysis of the unwholesome courses of action was known, so too the analysis of these wholesome courses of action (kusala-kammapatha) should be known by way of these five aspects: (1) by way of state (dhamma), (2) by way of portion (koṭṭhāsa), (3) by way of object (ārammaṇa), (4) by way of feeling (vedanā), and (5) by way of root (mūla).

Therein, the analysis 'by way of state' (dhamma) is as follows: Among these wholesome courses of action, in sequence, the first seven can be either volition (cetanā) or abstinence (virati). The final three are only states associated with volition.

The analysis 'by way of portion' (koṭṭhāsa) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven are only courses of action (kammapatha) and not roots (mūla). The final three are both courses of action and roots. When non-covetousness (anabhijjhā) reaches the level of a root, it becomes the wholesome root of non-greed (alobha-kusalamūla). Non-ill-will (abyāpāda) is the wholesome root of non-hatred (adosa-kusalamūla), and right view (sammā-diṭṭhi) is the wholesome root of non-delusion (amoha-kusalamūla).

The analysis 'by way of object' (ārammaṇa) is as follows: The objects of unwholesome states such as killing living beings are the very objects of these wholesome courses of action. This is because what is called 'abstinence' (veramaṇī) occurs only from the objective field that is to be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, which has Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, so too these courses of action, which have the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) and so forth as their objects, should be understood to abandon immoralities (dussīlya) such as killing living beings.

The analysis 'by way of feeling' (vedanā) is as follows: All courses of action are either accompanied by pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā) or neutral feeling (majjhatta-vedanā). This is because at the level of wholesome states, there is no such thing as painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

The analysis 'by way of root' (mūla) is as follows: In sequence, the first seven courses of action have three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta-citta). For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta-citta), there are two roots. When non-covetousness occurs with a consciousness associated with knowledge, it has two roots; when it occurs with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root. Non-greed itself cannot be its own root. The same method applies to non-ill-will. Right view has only two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. These are the ten wholesome courses of action.

## Discussion on the Comparison of Courses of Action

Now, at this point, what is called the comparison of the courses of action (kammapatha-saṃsandana) should be understood. Indeed, non-restraint (asaṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors (eye, ear, nose, tongue, body) is only unwholesome mental action (manokamma). However, non-restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door (manophassa-dvāra) can be all three types of action. If that non-restraint reaches the point of movement (copana) in the body-door, it is unwholesome bodily action (kāyakamma); if it reaches movement in the speech-door, it is unwholesome verbal action (vacīkamma); if it does not reach movement in either, it is unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the five doors of non-restraint is also only unwholesome mental action. Non-restraint arising by way of the body-door of non-restraint with movement is only unwholesome bodily action; that arising by way of the speech-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome verbal action; that arising by way of the mind-door of non-restraint is only unwholesome mental action. The three types of bodily misconduct are only unwholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal misconduct are only unwholesome verbal action; the three types of mental misconduct are only unwholesome mental action.

Restraint (saṃvara) arising by way of the five sense-contact doors is also only wholesome mental action. This restraint arising by way of the mind-contact door, like non-restraint, can be all three types of action. Restraint arising by way of the five doors of restraint is also only wholesome mental action; restraint arising by way of the body-door of restraint with movement is only wholesome bodily action; restraint arising by way of the speech-door of restraint is only wholesome verbal action; restraint arising by way of the mind-door of restraint is only wholesome mental action. The three types of bodily good conduct are only wholesome bodily action; the four types of verbal good conduct are only wholesome verbal action; the three types of mental good conduct are only wholesome mental action.

Unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors; it arises only by way of the mind-contact door. Unwholesome verbal action is the same. Unwholesome mental action, however, arises by way of all six sense-contact doors. If that mental action reaches movement in the body-door and speech-door, it becomes unwholesome bodily and verbal action; if it does not reach movement, it is only unwholesome mental action. Just as it does not arise by way of the five sense-contact doors, so too unwholesome bodily action does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises only by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome verbal action also does not arise by way of the five doors of non-restraint; it arises by way of the body-door and speech-door of non-restraint with movement, and not by way of the mind-door of non-restraint. Unwholesome mental action, however, certainly arises by way of the eight doors of non-restraint. The same method should be understood for wholesome bodily action and so forth.
149:
This is the distinction: just as unwholesome bodily and verbal actions do not arise by way of the door of mental non-restraint, these (wholesome bodily and verbal actions) are not like that. Indeed, these (wholesome actions) do arise even at the door of mental restraint for one who undertakes the precepts without moving the bodily or vocal organs.

Among those (doors), the wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta) arises by way of the three doors of action (kammadvara); it does not arise by way of the five doors of consciousness (viññāṇadvara). By the method, "Whatever feeling arises—whether pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant—conditioned by eye-contact," it arises by way of the six doors of contact (phassadvara). It does not arise by way of the eight doors of non-restraint (asaṃvaradvara); it arises by way of the eight doors of restraint (saṃvaradvara). It does not arise by way of the ten courses of unwholesome action (akusalakammapatha); it arises by way of the ten courses of wholesome action (kusalakammapatha). Therefore, whether this consciousness arises by way of the three doors of action, the six doors of contact, the eight doors of restraint, or the ten courses of wholesome action, it is so. When it is said, "A wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere has arisen ... etc. ... (taking) a visible object ... etc. ... or a mental object," everything has been stated.

## The Discussion on Doors is Finished.

Regarding the phrase "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha," the construction is as follows: among the visible objects and so forth mentioned below, it means "beginning with a visible object," or "having made it the object." It arises beginning with an audible object ... etc. ... or a mental object. By this much, it is as if only one of these objects is permitted for this consciousness. This (consciousness) arises for one person at one time beginning with a visible object, and again at another time for another person, it arises beginning with any other object among audible objects and so forth. For this consciousness thus arising, there is no such sequence as: first, in one existence, it arises beginning with a visible object, and later with an audible object. Even among visible objects, there is no such rule as: first a blue object, and later a yellow object.

Thus, to show the state of having all these as objects, the state of having no fixed sequence, and the state of having no fixed rule even among blue, yellow, and so forth despite the lack of sequence, he said, "yaṃ yaṃ vā panārabbha." This is the meaning: it is not just any single one among these visible objects and so forth; rather, it arises beginning with whichever object. Even when it arises thus, it does not occur in a sequence such as "first beginning with a visible object, then an audible object," but arises beginning with whichever object. The meaning is: "It arises by making this or that object among visible objects and so forth, whether in reverse order, in direct order, or by the method of skipping one, skipping two, and so forth."
